newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish C.Bank sees inflation at 1.75 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Irish C.Bank sees inflation at 1.75 pct in 1996.

text.p: The Central Bank of Ireland on Thursday cut its forecast for average Irish inflation in 1996 to 1.75 percent from 2.0 percent, and said it expected average inflation of 2.25 percent in 1997.
In its quarterly bulletin, the central bank left its forecast for 1996 GNP growth unchanged at 5.25 percent, adding that "a similar rate of growth is in prospect for 1997".
It warned that although the inflation situation was currently very favourable, "the medium term outlook looks less promising".

"The available indicators point to relatively muted inflationary pressures in the short-term but the continuation of strong growth is likely to put some upward pressure on prices in the medium term," the central bank said.

The central bank said that although there were signs that growth in the economy was moderating, 1996 would be the third year in succession that the economy's growth rate was above its long term potential.
"Estimates of the output gap -- the deviation of actual from potential output -- suggest that the economy is operating very close to full capacity," it said.
Strong domestic demand was also reflected in the accelerating growth of broad money and credit, the bank said.
"The rate of increase in house and property prices continues to be a concern," it said.
"Given the lags in the transmission of inflation, there is a greater risk of medium-term inflationary pressure than most short-term indicators suggest," the bank said.
It said the acceleration in Irish credit growth showed no sign of abating: "there is no sign of current trends being reversed".

The bank said wage restraint was crucial to help prevent the strong level of domestic demand having inflationary consequences. "Given the current strength of domestic demand, it is important that there be continued moderation in the rate of wage inflation," it said.

The bank noted that short-term money market rates had risen significantly over the summer months. "Some tightening of montetary conditions was warranted", it said, given the acceleration in credit growth and the importance of continued adherence to the Maastricht criteria over the next two years.
It said 1996 would be another year of strong employment growth, with total employment forecast to rise by 37,000. It forecast a fall in unemployment of 16,000 to 11.75 percent.
The volume of consumer spending was expected to rise about 4.5 percent in 1996, underpinned by strong income and employment growth and a stable financial environment, the bank said.

"The surplus on the balance of payments is expected to decline from 2.5 percent of GNP of GNP in 1995 to 1.5 percent in 1996, reflecting an increase in the services deficit and a rise in net factor payments," it said.
